int_name: N BROAD ST & W TIOGA ST

result.summary: The image depicts a wide urban roadway with multi-story commercial or institutional buildings. While basic pedestrian infrastructure like marked zebra crosswalks, sidewalks, and curb ramps are present, the significant crossing distance and wide travel lanes suggest a car-oriented design that may encourage higher vehicle speeds.

hazards.name: Long Crossing Distance
hazards.description: The wide roadway requires pedestrians to spend a significant amount of time exposed to traffic without a mid-crossing refuge.
hazards.location_in_image: Center foreground across the main roadway.

hazards.name: Wide Travel Lanes
hazards.description: The width of the travel lanes and the open street geometry likely encourage higher vehicle speeds.

interventions.title: Curb Extensions
interventions.description: Install bulb-outs at the corners to shorten the crossing distance and improve sight lines between drivers and pedestrians.

interventions.title: Pedestrian Refuge Island
interventions.description: Add a raised island in the center of the roadway to allow pedestrians to cross one direction of traffic at a time.

interventions.title: High-Visibility Pedestrian Signals
interventions.description: Install countdown pedestrian signals to provide clear information on crossing time remaining.

result.summary: The image shows a wide urban intersection with high-visibility continental crosswalks and signalized pedestrian controls. interventions.title: Curb Extensions
interventions.description: Install bulb-outs to shorten the crossing distance and improve visibility between drivers and pedestrians.

interventions.title: Leading Pedestrian Interval (LPI)
interventions.description: Program the traffic signals to give pedestrians a head start before vehicles get a green light.

result.summary: The street features a wide multi-lane roadway with a marked crosswalk but lacks a pedestrian refuge island or signalization. While sidewalks are in good condition, the long crossing distance and parked cars near the intersection create significant safety risks for pedestrians.

hazards.name: Long crossing distance
hazards.description: The wide roadway requires pedestrians to cross multiple lanes of traffic without a refuge, increasing exposure time.

hazards.name: Sightline obstruction
hazards.description: Parked cars on the right side of the street obstruct the view between drivers and pedestrians at the curb.

interventions.title: Pedestrian Refuge Island
interventions.description: Install a raised median island to allow pedestrians to cross one direction of traffic at a time.

interventions.title: Curb Extensions
interventions.description: Extend the sidewalk at the intersection to reduce crossing distance and improve pedestrian visibility.

interventions.title: Daylighting
interventions.description: Restrict parking near the crosswalk to ensure clear sightlines for both drivers and pedestrians.

result.summary: The pedestrian environment is currently compromised by active construction that obstructs the sidewalk and corner crossing area with barrels and fencing. While basic infrastructure like marked crosswalks and pedestrian signals are present, the physical barriers and uneven surfaces create significant navigation challenges and safety risks.

hazards.name: Sidewalk Obstruction
hazards.description: Construction barrels and orange fencing block the corner sidewalk area, forcing pedestrians into the roadway or onto uneven ground.

hazards.name: Uneven Surface
hazards.description: The sidewalk has been excavated or is covered in loose material within the construction zone, creating a trip hazard.

interventions.title: ADA-Compliant Temporary Pedestrian Path
interventions.description: Provide a clearly marked, level, and protected temporary walkway around the construction zone to maintain accessibility.

interventions.title: Pedestrian Detour Signage
interventions.description: Install signage ahead of the construction to inform pedestrians of the closure and direct them to the safest alternative crossing.
